title: Best Speech to Text Apps for Android (2026)
summary: The best speech to text apps for Android in 2026: what Gboard and Samsung voice typing do well, a free offline option, and the paid apps worth installing.
body_markdown:
Every Android phone can already turn speech into text. Tap the microphone on Gboard or Samsung Keyboard and it works in almost any app, in a long list of languages, often without a connection. So the real question is not whether you can dictate on Android, it is whether the built-in option is good enough for the writing you actually do on your phone, and what to install when it is not. This is a ranked shortlist for 2026: the free tools first, then five apps graded on one real reason each.


**The short answer:** start with Gboard voice typing (or Samsung Keyboard voice input on a Galaxy phone), which is free, already installed, and fine for texts and quick notes. If audio must never leave the phone, FUTO Voice Input is the free, open-source pick. For real work, Aqua Voice is the best speech to text app for Android: it floats above the keyboard you already use, so you never switch keyboards, and it lets you fix what you said by voice.


## First, the free speech to text your Android phone already has


### Gboard voice typing


Gboard is the default keyboard on most Android phones, and voice typing is built into it. According to Google's Gboard help page "Type with your voice", you open any app where you can type, tap a text field, and tap the **microphone** at the top of the keyboard. When you see "Speak now", say what you want written. To replace a word, touch and hold it, tap the microphone, and say the new word (our[talk to text on Android guide](https://aquavoice.com/blog/talk-to-text-android) covers the setup, commands, and fixes in full).


Punctuation is spoken: "period", "comma", "exclamation point", "question mark", "new line", and "new paragraph". Google notes that punctuation is not available in every language, that talk-to-text does not work with all languages, and that some steps need Android 7.0 or later. If you have more than one language enabled, you can switch between them from the voice toolbar.


On a Pixel 6 or later, Gboard adds what Google calls **advanced voice typing features** : tap Settings at the top of the keyboard, then **Voice typing** , and turn on **Advanced voice typing features** . With that on, the text you speak stays on the device, punctuation is added automatically as you talk, you can keep typing while the mic listens, and you can say "Send", "Clear", "Clear all", "Delete last word", "Next", and "Stop". Say an emoji's name ("smiley emoji") to insert it. Google lists English, French, German, Italian, Japanese, and Spanish for these features, and the "Fix it" and detailed-edit commands on Pixel 8 and later send your text to Google's servers, so they are the exception to the on-device rule.


### Samsung Keyboard voice input (Galaxy phones)


Galaxy phones ship with Samsung Keyboard, and Samsung's support page on keyboard settings describes two built-in voice-to-text options: **Samsung voice input** , which only works with Samsung Keyboard, and **Google voice typing** . To check what is enabled, open **Settings** , tap **General management** , then **Keyboard list and default** . To pick the engine, open Samsung Keyboard's settings and tap **Voice input** . Then, in any text field, tap the microphone on the keyboard's toolbar and talk. The same screen lets you install offline language packs, so dictation keeps working without a signal.


### Live Transcribe, for what other people say


If the job is captioning a conversation or a lecture rather than writing a message, Google's Live Transcribe is an accessibility app that shows speech on screen as text. Per Google's Android Accessibility help, it can download languages for offline use (on Pixel phones running Android 12 or later, and on some other devices), and it keeps your history for up to three days before deleting it. It is a transcriber, not a dictation tool: the text lands in the app, not in your email.


The built-in options are the right place to start. If one of them keeps up with you, you do not need anything below.


## What separates a good Android dictation app


Four things decide it on a phone. Pick the app that wins on the one you care about.


- **Accuracy on names, jargon, and the words you actually use.** Everyday sentences are a solved problem. The gap opens on product names, technical terms, and anything a general model has never heard. A tuned model plus a dictionary you can teach is what closes it.
- **Fixing mistakes without the cursor.** Selecting and correcting text on glass is the worst part of phone writing. An app that lets you fix or rewrite what you said by voice removes it.
- **Where the audio goes.** On-device (offline, private, no connection) versus cloud (heavier cleanup, needs a connection) is a real trade. Decide which side you are on before you pick.
- **The keyboard question.** On Android this one is different from iPhone. Some apps replace your keyboard, which means giving up Gboard's swipe typing or Samsung's layout. Others add a mic to your current keyboard, or float a button over it. The last design is the least disruptive, because nothing you already do changes.


## 1. Aqua Voice, best overall


We build Aqua Voice, so read this as informed rather than neutral, and judge the checkable claims for yourself.


[Aqua Voice for Android](https://aquavoice.com/android) is a button, not a keyboard. Tap into a text box in any app (Messages, Gmail, WhatsApp, Slack, Chrome, a ChatGPT or Claude chat) and the Aqua button appears above the keyboard you already use. Tap it, talk, and tap the checkmark; or hold it, talk, and let go. Clean text lands at the cursor, with filler words removed and punctuation in place, and Gboard or Samsung Keyboard stays exactly where it was. You can drag the button to either edge of the screen, drag it down to hide it for ten minutes, and shake the phone to bring it back. It never appears in password fields.


It runs on our own speech model,[Avalon](https://aquavoice.com/avalon-api) , rather than a general build. At its debut on the OpenASR leaderboard in October 2025, Avalon ranked as the top proprietary model (it now sits sixth overall as newer open models have landed). On the AISpeak benchmark Aqua reports 97.3% accuracy, a self-reported figure, so weigh it as one data point. The outside read is 9to5Mac, which ran the same passage through Apple's dictation and Aqua and counted 17 errors against 1; that test was run on Macs, so treat it as evidence about the model rather than the Android app. Text starts appearing in under 50 milliseconds, the final words land in about 450 milliseconds, and you can speak at up to 230 words per minute.


The reason it is first on a phone, though, is editing. Select text, tap **Edit** above the Aqua button, and say the change: "make this a list", "make it shorter", "change Thursday to Friday", "fix the grammar". Aqua rewrites the selection in place. That one feature removes the cursor-dragging that makes writing on a phone miserable. If you use[Edit Mode](https://aquavoice.com/blog/introducing-edit-mode) on a computer, it is the same idea, built for your thumb. A custom dictionary learns your names and terms, and your dictionary, replacements, and custom instructions sync with the[Mac](https://aquavoice.com/mac) ,[Windows](https://aquavoice.com/windows) , and[iPhone](https://aquavoice.com/ios) apps, so the setup you build on your laptop follows you to your phone. The desktop apps list 49 dictation languages; on Android, Aqua dictates in dozens of languages with an Auto-detect option, and the language picker in the app has the current list. Aqua is SOC 2 Type II compliant and ISO 27001 certified, and GDPR and HIPAA compliant for teams that need it.


Pricing is free for your first 1,000 words with no card required, then $8/mo billed annually, or $10 month-to-month, on the web;[paid plans](https://aquavoice.com/pricing) are also available in the app through Google Play, where billing may differ. One subscription covers Android, iPhone, Mac, and Windows. The[launch post](https://aquavoice.com/blog/aqua-voice-for-android) walks through setup, and the[guide](https://aquavoice.com/guide) covers the rest.[Get it on Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.aquavoice.android) .


The honest limits: Aqua transcribes in the cloud, so it needs a connection, and if your rule is that audio never leaves the phone, FUTO below is the better fit. It needs Android 10 or later and does not run on Android Go phones, which block floating buttons. Typing into other apps uses Android's accessibility permission, which setup explains and which you can review before granting. And the free tier is a one-time 1,000 words rather than an allowance that resets, so it is a trial, not a free plan.


## 2. FUTO Voice Input, best offline and open source


FUTO Voice Input is the pick when your voice should never leave the phone. The project's own README says it is "currently based on the OpenAI Whisper model", and FUTO's site describes it as designed to work entirely on-device with no data stored. The source is public under FUTO's Source First license, it is distributed through Google Play, F-Droid, and a direct APK, and the app itself is free, with an optional one-time license purchase to support the project. The UI offers the languages with the most Whisper training data, 17 at the time of writing, including English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Korean, and Chinese.


The catch is the keyboard question. FUTO Voice Input plugs into Android's voice-input slot, which open keyboards such as HeliBoard, FlorisBoard, AnySoftKeyboard, and the AOSP keyboard expose, along with SwiftKey; FUTO's own keyboard has it built in. But per the README, Gboard is hardcoded to Google's voice input and Samsung Keyboard only allows Samsung's or Google's, so on a stock phone you will be switching keyboards to use it. Accuracy is whatever the on-device Whisper model can do on your phone's hardware, and there is no cloud cleanup pass. If offline is your line in the sand and you are happy to change keyboards, this is the honest answer.


## 3. Typeless, best for heavy automatic cleanup


Typeless is for people who ramble and want the app to do the editing. Its own description is explicit about the job: it removes filler words and repetition, auto-edits when you change your mind mid-sentence, and auto-formats spoken lists and steps into structured text, across the apps you use on Mac, Windows, Linux, iPhone, and Android. It lists 100-plus languages, including mixing them in one dictation, with automatic language detection.


The trade is control and price. Heavy automatic rewriting is great when it guesses right and annoying when you wanted your exact words. At the time of writing, Pro is $12 a month billed yearly or $30 month-to-month, and the Free plan includes a limited number of words each week (Typeless does not publish the figure on its pricing page, so check it before you rely on it). Our[Aqua vs Typeless](https://aquavoice.com/vs/typeless) page has the detailed comparison.


## 4. Dragon Anywhere, best for existing Dragon users


If your office already runs Dragon on Windows, Dragon Anywhere is the mobile companion. Nuance describes it as professional-grade mobile dictation for creating and editing documents by voice, with continuous dictation and no word limits, a correction menu, trainable words, and custom words and auto-texts shared across your devices. It runs on Android 7.0 and later, and Nuance lists it as available in the US and Canada only.


The trade is that it is a document app with a subscription, not a system-wide tool: you dictate inside Dragon Anywhere and share the result out, it needs a Wi-Fi or cellular connection, and Nuance does not publish the subscription price on the product page, so check it before you commit. For most people who are not already in the Dragon ecosystem, the keyboard-level tools above are the better fit.


## 5. Wispr Flow, widest reach and a free allowance that resets


Wispr Flow's Android app takes the same approach as Aqua: per Wispr's Android page, Flow appears as a floating bubble whenever you are in a text field and works alongside your existing keyboard, with auto punctuation, filler-word removal, self-corrections, automatic numbered lists, and support for 100-plus languages. It requires Android 13 or later and an internet connection, and Wispr notes that tablets and foldables are supported but not yet optimized.


The reason to consider it is the free plan. At the time of writing, Wispr's pricing page lists 1,000 words a week on mobile (2,000 on desktop) on the Free plan, which resets, where Aqua's 1,000 free words do not. Pro is $12 per user a month billed annually or $15 month-to-month. Wispr does not disclose the speech model behind the app, so there is no public benchmark to compare it on, and opinions from long-term users on X are mixed. Our[Aqua vs Wispr Flow](https://aquavoice.com/vs/wispr-flow) page covers the head-to-head.


## How to choose


- **Texts, quick notes, and nothing fancy:** stay with Gboard or Samsung Keyboard voice input. It is free and already there.
- **Captioning what other people say:** Live Transcribe.
- **Audio must never leave the phone:** FUTO Voice Input, with a keyboard that supports it.
- **Real writing on your phone, with corrections by voice and no keyboard switch:** Aqua Voice.
- **You want the app to rewrite you as you go:** Typeless.
- **Your team already runs Dragon:** Dragon Anywhere.
- **A free allowance that resets every week:** Wispr Flow.


If you also write on a laptop, the pick matters more, because dictionary and settings sync is where the time saving compounds. Our cross-platform roundup of the[best dictation software](https://aquavoice.com/blog/best-dictation-software) covers Mac and Windows, the[iPhone roundup](https://aquavoice.com/blog/best-speech-to-text-app-for-iphone) is this article's sibling, and if you dictate into Google Docs on the phone, the[Google Docs voice typing guide](https://aquavoice.com/blog/google-docs-voice-typing) covers the browser side.


## FAQ


**Does Android have built-in speech to text?** Yes. Gboard voice typing is built into the default keyboard on most Android phones: tap the microphone at the top of the keyboard and talk. Galaxy phones also include Samsung voice input inside Samsung Keyboard. Both are free, and both can download languages for offline use.


**What is the most accurate speech to text app for Android?** It depends on what you say. For everyday sentences, Gboard is hard to beat for free. For names, jargon, and long-form writing, a tuned model with a custom dictionary pulls ahead; Aqua's Avalon model ranked as the top proprietary model at its October 2025 OpenASR debut, and its 97.3% AISpeak figure is self-reported, so test it on your own words with the free 1,000-word allowance.


**Can I use speech to text offline on Android?** Yes. Gboard and Samsung Keyboard can download offline language packs, and Pixel 6 and later phones process advanced voice typing on the device. FUTO Voice Input runs an open-source Whisper model entirely on the phone. Cloud apps such as Aqua, Typeless, Wispr Flow, and Dragon Anywhere need a connection.


**Do I have to switch keyboards to use a dictation app on Android?** Not always. Aqua Voice and Wispr Flow float a button over whatever keyboard you already use, so Gboard or Samsung Keyboard stays. FUTO Voice Input needs a keyboard that exposes Android's voice-input slot, which Gboard and Samsung Keyboard do not, so it usually means a keyboard change.
